We recommend [**Positron**](https://positron.posit.co/) as your IDE for this course. It is built on VS Code, so the interface and shortcuts will feel familiar if you come from Python. It has a dedicated Variables pane, an integrated R console, and first-class support for both R and Python in the same project.

:::{.callout-tip}
## R for Python users

| Python | R | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `x = 5` | `x <- 5` | `<-` is the conventional assignment in R; `=` works but is avoided at the top level |
| `import numpy as np` | `library(terra)` | Load packages with `library()`, install once with `install.packages("terra")` |
| `a[0]` | `a[1]` | R is **1-indexed** |
| `df.pivot(...)` | `pivot_wider(...)` | Reshaping is done with `tidyr` functions |
| `df.method()` chaining | `df \|> func()` | R uses the native pipe `\|>` to chain operations |
| `None` / `float('nan')` | `NA` | R uses `NA` for all missing values; most functions have an `na.rm = TRUE` argument |
| `arr.shape` | `dim(x)`, `nrow(x)`, `ncol(x)` | No single `.shape`; use `dim()` for the full dimensions |
:::

## Tip: pipes and tidyverse

The `|>` pipe passes the left-hand result as the **first argument** of the next function — equivalent to writing nested calls, but readable left-to-right. If you know pandas method chaining (`.groupby().agg()`), the mental model is the same.

`tidyr` and `dplyr` together are R's closest equivalent to pandas: 

- `pivot_wider()` ~ `df.pivot()`
- `select()` ~ `df[["col"]]`
- `filter()` ~ `df[df.x > 0]`
- `mutate()` ~ `df["new"] = ...`.
:::

## Task 5

The following command returns the path to a GeoTIFF file on your hard drive:

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Tip: terra vs rasterio / numpy

`terra` is R's primary raster package. If you have used `rasterio` or `numpy` arrays for raster data in Python, here is a rough mapping:

| Python | R (terra) |
|---|---|
| `rasterio.open("f.tif")` | `rast("f.tif")` |
| `src.read()` → numpy array | `values(r)` → matrix |
| `src.meta` | print the `SpatRaster` object |
| `src.crs` | `crs(r)` |
| `src.transform` / `src.res` | `res(r)`, `ext(r)` |

Unlike a raw numpy array, a `SpatRaster` keeps its spatial metadata (CRS, extent, resolution) attached at all times.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="false"}
system.file("ex/elev.tif", package = "terra")
```
:::


Use this path to import the file using `rast()`, store it as `r`.


::: {.cell}

:::

## Task 12

Check whether `r` uses a geographic or projected CRS. Reproject it to EPSG:2169 (Luxembourg national projection) and compare `res()` before and after.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Tip: CRS and reprojection

In Python you would use `pyproj.CRS` or `geopandas`/`rasterio`'s `.to_crs()`. In `terra`, `project(r, "EPSG:2169")` handles both the coordinate transform and the pixel resampling in one step. A geographic CRS (degrees) will show `res()` values around `0.008`, while a projected CRS (metres) will show values in the hundreds — same pixel, different units.
:::


::: {.cell}

:::
